description: mSCP to ASD ISM 'supports' mappings that were not certain enough to commit. A later research pass adds a comment to each item and sets its status; whatever stays uncertain goes to the maintainer to decide.

statuses.open: not yet researched beyond the first pass
statuses.rejected: researched and found not to support the control
statuses.needs_maintainer: still uncertain after research; the maintainer makes the call (the last comment holds the question)
statuses.answered: a cross-cutting question that has been settled

cross_cutting_questions.question: Do Mac laptops count as ISM 'mobile devices'? If so, several Guidelines for enterprise mobility controls (e.g. ISM-0682, ISM-0864, ISM-0869, ISM-1366, ISM-1888, ISM-2096, ISM-1482) gain candidate mappings, most of which the first pass left out entirely.

comments.comment: Yes for laptops. The ISM glossary (Cyber security terminology, https://www.cyber.gov.au/ism/latest/cyber-security-terminology, read 2026-10-30) defines a mobile device as 'A portable computing or communications device. For example, smartphones, tablets and laptop computers.' The definition is OS-agnostic, so Mac laptops are treated the same as Windows laptops: mobile device controls apply to MacBooks, not to desktop Macs (iMac, Mac mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro). Notes on mobile device mappings should say they apply to Mac laptops.

cross_cutting_questions.question: Does APFS/FileVault encryption (AES-XTS) count as 'ASD-approved cryptography' (ISM-1059 and similar)? AES is an ASD-approved algorithm, but the control may expect an evaluated implementation at higher classifications.

comments.comment: Yes. FileVault encrypts with AES-XTS-256 (NIAP validation report CCEVS-VR-VID11696-2026, 'Apple macOS 26 Tahoe: FileVault', completed 2026-07-29, evaluated against the collaborative Protection Profiles for Full Drive Encryption - Authorization Acquisition and Encryption Engine v2.0), and AES-256 is an ASD-Approved Cryptographic Algorithm (ISM-1769, ISM-1770). The maintainer accepts FileVault/APFS encryption as ASD-approved cryptography; FileVault is also the only full disk encryption macOS supports.

cross_cutting_questions.question: Should rules that only attest to built-in macOS behaviour (no check and no fix) ever be mapped? The first pass left almost all of them unmapped, even near word-for-word matches such as os_unique_identification to ISM-0414.

comments.comment: Maintainer ruling: for now, only map rules that have a check or a fix. Attestation-only rules stay unmapped.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device usage > Using paging, message services and messaging apps
items.ism_text: Paging, Multimedia Message Service, Short Message Service and messaging apps are not used to communicate sensitive or classified data.
items.proposed_note: Blocks Apple Messages only; other messaging apps, and SMS/MMS on other devices, are not covered.

comments.rationale: Preventing Messages.app from launching stops that messaging app being used on the Mac, which supports 'messaging apps are not used to communicate sensitive or classified data'.
comments.open_question: The control is a usage restriction on sensitive data rather than a ban on apps; a reviewer may consider blocking one app too indirect to count.

comments.comment: Read both rules. os_messages_app_disable denies com.apple.MobileSMS through the supported DDM app settings declaration, while the familycontrols variant uses the deprecated pathBlackList key, so only the first is dependable. Preventing the app from launching directly prevents its use, and Mac laptops are mobile devices (ruling 1). Source: https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.new.yaml

items.final_note: Blocks the Apple Messages app from launching on Mac laptops, so that messaging app cannot be used to send sensitive or classified data; other messaging apps and SMS/MMS are not covered.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: If there is no business requirement for writing to removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces.
items.proposed_note: Covers blocking writes to optical media (blank discs and DVD-RAM ejected, CD and Blu-ray mounted read-only), using a configuration key Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls set blankcd/blankdvd/blankbd/dvdram to alert/eject and cd/bd to read-only, which would disable 'writing to removable media' for optical media.
comments.open_question: Each rule warns that Apple has deprecated media mount-controls and they 'may not work as expected'; confirm the controls are enforced on current macOS (or that third-party device control is used instead).

comments.comment: All six rules rely on com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls. Apple's device-management schema marks this payload deprecated as of macOS 11 (no removal version listed) and each rule's own text warns it may not work as expected. I found no primary source confirming it is still enforced, and the check only reads the preference rather than proving writes are blocked. The supported DDM ExternalStorage restriction (r003) covers the same intent. Source: https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.systemuiserver.yaml

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: If there is no business requirement for writing to removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces.
items.proposed_note: Covers blocking writes to external storage only when the organisation sets the value to ReadOnly or Disallowed.

comments.rationale: The DDM disk management ExternalStorage restriction (Allowed|ReadOnly|Disallowed) is verified against the organisation-defined value; ReadOnly or Disallowed disables 'writing to removable media and devices'.
comments.open_question: The rule's recommended value is Allowed, which provides no support; the mapping only holds where the organisation sets ReadOnly or Disallowed.

comments.comment: The rule verifies the DDM disk management ExternalStorage value against the organisation-defined value. ReadOnly or Disallowed disables writing to removable media, which is the control's intent where there is no business need.

items.final_note: Blocks or limits writing to external storage when the organisation sets the ExternalStorage restriction to ReadOnly or Disallowed; the Allowed value gives no coverage.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: If there is no business requirement for writing to removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces.
items.proposed_note: Blocks mounting of external hard disks only, using a control Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: Ejecting external disks on connect also prevents writing to them, matching 'If there is no business requirement for writing to removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled'.
comments.open_question: Same as for ism-1418: confirm the deprecated mount-controls payload still takes effect.

comments.comment: Uses the deprecated com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls payload (deprecated macOS 11 per Apple's schema, https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.systemuiserver.yaml), which the rule warns may not work; the check only reads the preference. Rejected for the same reason as r002; r003 is the supported equivalent.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: External communication interfaces that allow DMA are disabled.
items.proposed_note: Blocks newly connected USB/Thunderbolt accessories until approved and while the Mac is locked; it does not disable the interfaces.

comments.rationale: Accessory security stops new USB-C/Thunderbolt devices communicating with a locked Mac, which mitigates the locked-device DMA attack described in the control's discussion, but it does not meet 'External communication interfaces that allow DMA are disabled'.
comments.open_question: Whether a 'block until authorised / while locked' restriction counts as partial support for a control whose wording requires the DMA-capable interface to be disabled.

comments.comment: The check passes whenever allowUSBRestrictedMode is not forced false, so it does not verify active enforcement. The feature blocks new accessories until approved or while locked; it does not disable DMA-capable interfaces, so it does not meet ISM-0345 even in part.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of operating systems are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Covers blocking the bundled Calendar.app or FaceTime.app, but through a configuration method Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: These variants block /Applications/Calendar.app and /Applications/FaceTime.app via the legacy familyControlsEnabled/pathBlackList keys, which would disable that bundled OS functionality as ISM-0380 asks ('functionality of operating systems are disabled').
comments.open_question: Apple has deprecated the com.apple.applicationaccess.new path blacklist; confirm it is still honoured on the targeted macOS versions before treating it as enforcing anything.

comments.comment: Both rules install the deprecated pathBlackList key (Apple: deprecated since macOS 10.15, use pathDenyList; https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.new.yaml). The Calendar and FaceTime checks also read com.apple.alr while the profile writes com.apple.applicationaccess.new, a mismatch reported in usnistgov/macos_security issue 842, so the check does not test what the fix sets.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of operating systems are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Covers disabling the mounting of disk images, using a configuration key Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: Sets com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls disk-image to alert/eject so disk images cannot be mounted, which disables a piece of operating system functionality ('functionality of operating systems are disabled').
comments.open_question: The rule itself warns that Apple has deprecated media mount-controls and they 'may not work as expected'; confirm enforcement on current macOS.

comments.comment: Uses the deprecated com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls payload (deprecated macOS 11; https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.systemuiserver.yaml) which the rule says may not work; the check only reads the preference, so enforcement is unproven.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of operating systems are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Blocks the bundled Mail and Messages apps from launching; covers only those two apps.

comments.rationale: Configuration profiles block /Applications/Mail.app and Messages (com.apple.MobileSMS) from launching, disabling 'components ... of operating systems'.
comments.open_question: Whether the organisation deems these apps unneeded (the Mail rule itself allows Mail where it is an approved email tool), and whether bundled apps count as operating system components rather than user applications (ISM-1470).

comments.comment: Ruling 5 supports disabling a feature under ISM-0380 where the organisation deems it unneeded. os_messages_app_disable uses the supported DDM app settings declaration; os_mail_app_disable and the familycontrols variant use pathBlackList, deprecated since macOS 10.15 (Apple: https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.new.yaml), hence the caveat in the note.

Research proposed mapping with note: Blocks the bundled Messages and Mail apps from launching, where the organisation has decided those apps are unneeded; Messages is blocked through a supported DDM declaration, the Mail block uses a key Apple has deprecated, and no other apps are covered. Held for the maintainer: Is a bundled-app block that relies on the deprecated pathBlackList key (Mail) acceptable support for ISM-0380, when other items using deprecated keys were rejected?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of operating systems are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Turns off one data-sharing-with-Apple option; this is closer to a privacy setting than removal of an OS component or service.

comments.rationale: The rules disable sending diagnostics, voice/search/Siri improvement data and ad personalisation. The rule text frames them as 'provide only essential capabilities', which echoes 'unneeded ... functionality', but they are preference opt-outs rather than disabling a component or service. Test applied to every disable-a-feature rule for ism-0380: confident when the rule turns off an OS service that accepts inbound connections or access from other devices or people (a sharing/remote-access listener or a built-in account), because removing such a service is the core of the control; unsure when it turns off a client-side feature or a data-sharing preference, because whether that counts as 'unneeded ... functionality' is a per-organisation business decision rather than an attack-surface consensus.
comments.open_question: Whether a reviewer accepts telemetry and data-sharing opt-outs as 'functionality of operating systems' under ism-0380, rather than as data-handling or privacy measures outside this control.

comments.comment: Each rule has a check and a profile fix that disables a feature. Ruling 5 says disabling a feature supports ISM-0380, so these opt-outs qualify.

Research proposed mapping with note: Turns off a diagnostics, voice, search, Siri dictation or ad personalisation data-sharing option, where the organisation has decided that feature is unneeded. Held for the maintainer: Do telemetry and data-sharing opt-outs (diagnostics, 'improve' settings) count as disabling unneeded OS functionality under ISM-0380, or are they privacy settings outside it?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for cryptography > Secure Shell > Authentication mechanisms
items.ism_text: Public key-based authentication is used for SSH connections.
items.proposed_note: Would cover removing password-based SSH logon, which leaves public key authentication as the main remaining method.

comments.rationale: Setting PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no in sshd removes password-based methods. The control says 'public key-based authentication is used for SSH connections', but this rule does not itself enable or require public key authentication, and other methods (for example GSSAPI/Kerberos) are not addressed.
comments.open_question: Check whether, with these two settings disabled on macOS sshd, public key is effectively the only enabled method, or whether another rule must also confirm PubkeyAuthentication and disable GSSAPI.

comments.comment: The check counts passwordauthentication no and kbdinteractiveauthentication no in sshd -G (both required) and the fix writes them to sshd_config. With both off, public key authentication is the remaining logon method on macOS sshd, which matches the control's intent.

items.final_note: Disables password and keyboard-interactive SSH logon, leaving public key authentication as the way to log on over SSH.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for security assurance > Security monitoring > Event log details
items.ism_text: For each event logged, the date and time of the event, the relevant user or process, the relevant filename, the event description, and the information technology equipment involved are captured.
items.proposed_note: macOS audit records include date and time, user and process, file path and event type; whether the device is identified in each record is not confirmed.

comments.rationale: With auditd enabled, each BSM record carries a header token (event type and timestamp), a subject token (audit user, effective user and process ID) and path tokens for file events, covering 'date and time of the event, the relevant user or process, the relevant filename, the event description'. The 'information technology equipment involved' is not obviously in each record.
comments.open_question: Whether BSM records include a host identifier (for example a header_ex or subject_ex address, or the audit host setting), or whether the device is only identified by the collecting system.

comments.comment: The rule verifies the auditd service is enabled; BSM records carry a header (event and time), subject (user and process) and path tokens. Partial coverage is acceptable and the note says which parts.

items.final_note: Enables the macOS audit daemon so events are recorded with date and time, user and process, event type, and file path where the configured audit flags cover file events; identifying the device is not confirmed.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device usage > Using Bluetooth functionality
items.ism_text: Bluetooth functionality is not enabled on SECRET and TOP SECRET mobile devices.
items.proposed_note: Turns Bluetooth off on the Mac; relevant only to SECRET and TOP SECRET Mac laptops.

comments.rationale: The rule sets DisableBluetooth, which directly meets 'Bluetooth functionality is not enabled on SECRET and TOP SECRET mobile devices'.
comments.open_question: The mechanism is a direct match; the open point is whether the organisation treats MacBooks as ISM 'mobile devices' (the ISM glossary is understood to include laptops, but no glossary is in the repo to verify this).

comments.comment: DisableBluetooth directly matches the control and Mac laptops are mobile devices (ruling 1).

Research proposed mapping with note: Turns Bluetooth off on SECRET and TOP SECRET Mac laptops (mobile devices); not needed below those classifications. Held for the maintainer: The rule turns Bluetooth off but still allows it while an approved device is connected; does that support 'Bluetooth functionality is not enabled' on SECRET and TOP SECRET laptops?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Application control
items.ism_text: Application control is implemented on workstations.
items.proposed_note: Covers Gatekeeper's check that apps are signed by an Apple-issued developer certificate before they run, which is not a full organisation-approved application allowlist.

comments.rationale: EnableAssessment=true turns on Gatekeeper, which blocks unsigned or un-notarised apps at launch, a form of execution control on workstations ('application control is implemented on workstations').
comments.open_question: ISM application control means restricting execution to an organisation-approved set (see ISM-1657); Gatekeeper permits any Apple-signed developer and admins can override it, so decide whether it counts as application control at all.

comments.comment: ISM-0843 lists publisher certificate rules as an accepted application control method, while preferring organisation-defined rulesets. Gatekeeper is partial coverage and the note states the limit so the reader can decide the fit.

Research proposed mapping with note: Turns on Gatekeeper so only apps signed by an Apple-issued certificate run; this is publisher-signature based and is not an organisation-approved allowlist. Held for the maintainer: Gatekeeper allows any Apple-signed developer, not an organisation-approved set; does it support 'application control is implemented', even partially?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Application control
items.ism_text: Application control is implemented on workstations.
items.proposed_note: Gatekeeper only allows App Store or Apple Developer ID signed apps; it is not an organisation-approved allowlist.

comments.rationale: Gatekeeper restricts execution to code signed by Apple-issued certificates, a form of publisher-based execution control related to 'Application control is implemented on workstations'. ISM application control (see ism-1657) means restricting execution to an organisation-approved set, which Gatekeeper does not do, and admins can override per app.
comments.open_question: Whether Gatekeeper's signed-code requirement is accepted as partial support for application control, or treated as a separate code-signing control with no ISM equivalent.

comments.comment: Same reasoning as r013: ISM-0843 accepts publisher certificate rules, and the setting restricts execution to a publisher class, but not to an organisation-approved set.

Research proposed mapping with note: Limits execution to apps from the App Store or signed by Apple Developer ID; this is publisher-signature based and is not an organisation-approved allowlist. Held for the maintainer: Gatekeeper allows any Apple-signed developer, not an organisation-approved set; does it support 'application control is implemented', even partially?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Session termination
items.ism_text: Interactive user sessions are terminated and workstations are restarted at least daily.
items.proposed_note: Logs out sessions idle for ODV seconds (86400 recommended); an active user is never logged out and no daily restart is forced.

comments.rationale: Auto logout after 24 hours of inactivity terminates abandoned interactive sessions, which is part of 'Interactive user sessions are terminated and workstations are restarted at least daily', but it is inactivity-based rather than a daily termination and it does not restart the workstation.
comments.open_question: Whether an inactivity-based logout is accepted as partial support for a control that requires termination at least daily regardless of activity, plus a restart.

comments.comment: The rule sets the idle logout delay (86400 recommended), which ends abandoned sessions. It covers only part of the control's daily termination and restart requirement, which the note states.

Research proposed mapping with note: Logs out sessions idle for the configured time (at most 86400 seconds); active sessions are not terminated and no daily restart is forced. Held for the maintainer: An idle-based logout never ends active sessions or restarts the Mac; does it support the daily terminate-and-restart control?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted storage
items.ism_text: Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage and any removable media using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Covers internal storage encryption on Mac laptops only (desktops are not mobile devices), and does not verify ASD-approved cryptography or removable media.

comments.rationale: Requiring all internal APFS user volumes to be encrypted matches 'Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage' when the Mac is a laptop.
comments.open_question: Whether Mac laptops are in scope as 'mobile devices' for this control, and whether APFS encryption counts as ASD-approved cryptography.

comments.comment: Check and fix require all internal user APFS volumes encrypted. Mac laptops are mobile devices (ruling 1) and FileVault/APFS encryption counts as approved cryptography (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Requires internal APFS storage to be encrypted on Mac laptops (mobile devices) using ASD-approved cryptography; removable media is not covered.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted storage
items.ism_text: Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage and any removable media using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Encrypts the Mac's internal storage; removable media are not covered.

comments.rationale: For Mac laptops, FileVault meets 'Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage ... using ASD-approved cryptography' for the internal storage part.
comments.open_question: Two points: whether the organisation treats MacBooks as ISM 'mobile devices' (the ISM glossary is understood to include laptops, but no glossary is in the repo to verify this), and whether FileVault counts as ASD-approved cryptography.

comments.comment: Mac laptops are mobile devices (ruling 1) and FileVault is accepted as ASD-approved cryptography (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Turns on FileVault to encrypt internal storage on Mac laptops (mobile devices) with ASD-approved cryptography; removable media is not covered.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Enterprise mobility > Mobile devices and desktop computers accessing the internet
items.ism_text: Mobile devices and desktop computers access the internet via an organisation’s internet gateway rather than via a direct connection to the internet.
items.proposed_note: Prevents Safari and unencrypted app traffic from being tunnelled through Apple's relays past the organisation's gateway controls; it does not route the device's internet traffic via the organisation's gateway.

comments.rationale: With allowCloudPrivateRelay forced false, Private Relay cannot wrap browsing traffic in Apple's relay, which would otherwise hide destinations from the organisation's internet gateway (web content filtering, protective DNS) that the control's discussion relies on. The control's words 'access the internet via an organisation's internet gateway' still need a VPN or network design to be met.
comments.open_question: Whether a setting that only removes one bypass of gateway inspection counts as supporting this control, given the control is about routing all internet access through the organisation's gateway.

comments.comment: allowCloudPrivateRelay=false removes a path that bypasses gateway filtering and DNS controls, supporting access via the organisation's gateway. Partial coverage, stated in the note.

Research proposed mapping with note: Disables iCloud Private Relay so browsing traffic is not tunnelled past the organisation's internet gateway; it does not itself route traffic through the gateway. Held for the maintainer: Disabling iCloud Private Relay removes one way around the gateway but does not route traffic through it; is that support for ISM-0874?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Covers verifying that attached external APFS and HFS+ volumes are encrypted; other file systems such as FAT and exFAT are not checked.

comments.rationale: The check lists external APFS/HFS+ volumes with diskutil and fails if any reports FileVault: No, i.e. it verifies 'all data stored on media is encrypted' for those volumes using APFS/FileVault AES encryption.
comments.open_question: Whether APFS/HFS+ volume encryption (AES-XTS) counts as 'ASD-approved cryptography' for the classification in scope; also FAT and exFAT volumes are not checked.

comments.comment: The check lists external APFS/HFS+ volumes and fails on any unencrypted one. APFS encryption counts as ASD-approved (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Verifies attached external APFS and HFS+ volumes are encrypted with ASD-approved cryptography; FAT and exFAT volumes are not checked.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Ensures data on internal Mac storage is encrypted, but does not verify the cryptography is ASD-approved and does not cover removable media.

comments.rationale: Encrypting all internal user APFS volumes means data stored on that media is encrypted, matching 'All data stored on media is encrypted'.
comments.open_question: Whether Apple's APFS/FileVault AES-XTS implementation counts as 'ASD-approved cryptography' (approved algorithm versus evaluated implementation).

comments.comment: Check and fix require internal APFS volumes encrypted; APFS encryption counts as ASD-approved (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Requires data on internal Mac storage to be encrypted with ASD-approved cryptography; removable media is not covered.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Covers data on the internal startup disk only.

comments.rationale: FileVault enforced at setup encrypts the internal data volume with AES-XTS, which supports 'All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography' for that disk.
comments.open_question: Confirm FileVault's AES-XTS (AES-128 block cipher with a 256-bit XTS key) counts as ASD-approved for the classification in scope, and whether checking the ForceEnableInSetupAssistant key rather than fdesetup status is adequate evidence.

comments.comment: Check reads ForceEnableInSetupAssistant and the fix sets it; it enforces encryption at setup rather than verifying current disk state, which is partial but sufficient to support the control. FileVault is approved cryptography (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Forces FileVault to be turned on during Setup Assistant so data on the internal startup disk is encrypted with ASD-approved cryptography.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Encrypts data on the Mac's internal storage with AES-XTS; removable media are not covered.

comments.rationale: FileVault encrypts internal storage with AES-XTS, supporting 'All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography' for the internal drive.
comments.open_question: Whether FileVault (AES-XTS with keys protected by the Secure Enclave) is accepted as 'ASD-approved cryptography' for the classification in question; AES is an ASD-approved algorithm but higher classifications may require an evaluated implementation.

comments.comment: FileVault is accepted as ASD-approved cryptography (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Turns on FileVault so data on the Mac's internal storage is encrypted with ASD-approved cryptography; removable media is not covered.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Checks that Time Machine backup volumes are encrypted; other media are not covered.

comments.rationale: Encrypted Time Machine destinations mean backup data stored on that media is encrypted, part of 'All data stored on media is encrypted using ASD-approved cryptography'.
comments.open_question: Whether Time Machine's encryption (APFS, AES-XTS) is accepted as ASD-approved cryptography; the rule is also manual-fix only.

comments.comment: The rule has a check (no NotEncrypted entries in the Time Machine preferences) and a documented manual fix, so it qualifies under ruling 4. APFS encryption counts as approved (ruling 2).

items.final_note: Checks that Time Machine backup volumes are encrypted with ASD-approved cryptography; other media are not covered, and the fix is manual.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Security updates are applied to mobile devices as soon as they become available.
items.proposed_note: Automatically installs macOS security updates on Mac laptops.

comments.rationale: Automatic installation of security updates is the mechanism for 'Security updates are applied to mobile devices as soon as they become available'.
comments.open_question: Two points: whether the organisation treats MacBooks as ISM 'mobile devices' (the ISM glossary is understood to include laptops, but no glossary is in the repo to verify this), and whether automatic installation is accepted as 'as soon as they become available' given deferrals and restarts.

comments.comment: Mac laptops are mobile devices (ruling 1). Automatic installation is the mechanism for applying security updates promptly; the note flags the restart caveat.

items.final_note: Automatically installs macOS security updates on Mac laptops (mobile devices); installation may still depend on user restarts.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Application control
items.ism_text: When implementing application control using path rules, only approved users can modify approved files and write to approved folders.
items.proposed_note: Relevant only when application control uses path rules on /Applications.

comments.rationale: The rule finds and removes world-writable permissions on apps in /Applications, so only owners or admins can modify them, supporting 'only approved users can modify approved files and write to approved folders'.
comments.open_question: Only applies if application control path rules include /Applications; removing world-write does not by itself restrict writes to 'approved users'.

comments.comment: The check and fix find and correct world-writable apps, so only owners and administrators can modify files in that approved path, which is the control's concern for path rules.

items.final_note: Removes world-writable permissions from apps in /Applications; relevant where application control uses path rules covering /Applications.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > User account lockouts
items.ism_text: User accounts, except for break glass accounts, are protected by fixed or risk-based lockout mechanisms aligned to a maximum of five failed logon attempts, with either indefinite or automated lockout durations.
items.proposed_note: Would cover the lockout duration part of the control; the control accepts any automated duration, so this only confirms one is configured.

comments.rationale: minutesUntilFailedLoginReset / autoEnableInSeconds sets how long an account stays locked after the failed-attempt limit, matching 'with either indefinite or automated lockout durations'. It does not set the attempt threshold, which is the substantive requirement of the control.
comments.open_question: Decide whether configuring the lockout duration counts as supporting a control that permits any duration, or whether only the attempt-threshold rule should map.

comments.comment: Check and fix enforce an organisation-defined lockout duration (minimum 1 minute, recommended 15). The control accepts indefinite or automated durations, so configuring an automated duration directly supports it.

items.final_note: Sets how long an account stays locked after failed logons (at least 15 minutes recommended); the failed-attempt limit of five is set by a separate rule.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Software firewall
items.ism_text: A software firewall is implemented on workstations and servers to restrict inbound and outbound network connections to an organisation-approved set of applications and services.
items.proposed_note: Covers verifying that the built-in pf packet filter has an inbound default-deny rule; outbound restriction and restricting by approved application are not verified.

comments.rationale: The check requires 'block drop in all' in the active pf ruleset, which is a software firewall on the workstation restricting inbound network connections, i.e. part of 'restrict inbound and outbound network connections'.
comments.open_question: pf allows traffic by port and host rather than by application, and the check only proves an inbound default-deny exists; decide whether that is enough to call it support for 'an organisation-approved set of applications and services'.

comments.comment: The check requires a block drop in all rule in the active pf ruleset. This is a software firewall restricting inbound connections, which is partial coverage of the control.

items.final_note: Verifies the pf firewall has an inbound default-deny rule; outbound restriction and approval by application are not verified.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Software firewall
items.ism_text: A software firewall is implemented on workstations and servers to restrict inbound and outbound network connections to an organisation-approved set of applications and services.
items.proposed_note: Stealth mode stops the Mac answering unsolicited probes; it hardens the software firewall rather than restricting connections to approved applications.

comments.rationale: Stealth mode makes the Application Firewall drop probes (e.g. ICMP ping, closed-port responses), a refinement of the inbound filtering in ism-1416, but it does not itself restrict connections 'to an organisation-approved set of applications and services'.
comments.open_question: Whether a firewall hardening option, rather than the restriction itself, should be counted as supporting ism-1416.

comments.comment: Stealth mode only stops the Application Firewall answering probes such as ICMP and closed-port responses. It does not restrict connections to an approved set of applications and services, so it is a hardening option rather than support for the control; the firewall-enable and default-deny rules cover the actual restriction.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Antivirus application
items.ism_text: An antivirus application is implemented on workstations and servers with:
items.proposed_note: Covers automatic installation of XProtect and Gatekeeper definition updates, which helps keep antivirus signatures current.

comments.rationale: ConfigDataInstall=true makes Software Update install XProtect Remediator and Gatekeeper data automatically, supporting the sub-requirement 'detection signatures configured to update at least daily'.
comments.open_question: Automatic install does not guarantee updates 'at least daily' as the control requires; confirm Apple's update cadence and check interval before treating this as meeting that bullet.

comments.comment: ISM-1417 lists signatures updating at least daily. ConfigDataInstall=true makes macOS install security data updates automatically, a partial but direct contribution.

items.final_note: Automatically installs XProtect and Gatekeeper data updates, supporting the antivirus requirement that detection signatures update at least daily; the cadence itself is set by Apple.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: If there is no business requirement for reading from removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces.
items.proposed_note: Covers blocking reads from external storage only when the organisation sets the value to Disallowed.

comments.rationale: The DDM disk management ExternalStorage restriction set to Disallowed prevents external storage from mounting, disabling 'reading from removable media and devices'.
comments.open_question: The rule's recommended value is Allowed; the mapping only holds where the organisation chooses Disallowed.

comments.comment: Disallowed prevents external storage mounting, disabling reading from removable media where there is no business need.

items.final_note: Blocks reading from external storage when the organisation sets the ExternalStorage restriction to Disallowed; other values give no coverage.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Device access control
items.ism_text: If there is no business requirement for reading from removable media and devices, such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces.
items.proposed_note: Blocks mounting of external hard disks only, using a control Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: The rule sets com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls harddisk-external to alert and eject so external disks are not mounted, which would disable reading from removable media as in 'such functionality is disabled via the use of a device access control application or by disabling external communication interfaces'.
comments.open_question: The rule itself warns Apple deprecated media mount controls and they may not work; confirm they still take effect on the target macOS versions.

comments.comment: Uses the deprecated com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls payload (deprecated macOS 11; https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.systemuiserver.yaml), which the rule warns may not work; the check only reads the preference. r030 is the supported equivalent.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > User application hardening > Hardening user application configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of user applications are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Disables specific off-device AI and cloud lookup features inside Mail, Notes, Calendar/Reminders and Photos; covers only those features.

comments.rationale: Restrictions (allowMailSmartReplies, allowMailSummary, allowNotesTranscription, allowNotesTranscriptionSummary, Calendar AllowNaturalLanguageEditing, IPXDefaultEnhancedVisualSearchEnabled all false) disable functionality of user applications, matching 'Unneeded ... functionality of user applications are disabled or removed'.
comments.open_question: Whether the organisation deems these features unneeded (the rules disable them unless explicitly approved), and whether Apple-bundled apps are treated as user applications (ISM-1470) rather than OS components (ISM-0380).

comments.comment: Each rule restricts a feature of a bundled user application via a profile with a check, matching ISM-1470 and the logic of ruling 5 for disabled features. The note scopes it to organisations that deem the features unneeded.

items.final_note: Disables specific off-device AI and cloud features in Mail, Notes, Calendar or Photos, where the organisation has decided those features are unneeded.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > User application hardening > Hardening user application configurations
items.ism_text: Unneeded user accounts, components, services and functionality of user applications are disabled or removed.
items.proposed_note: Disables the off-device Safari summary feature only.

comments.rationale: The rule sets allowSafariSummary=false (and the intelligence DDM declaration), disabling a Safari feature that sends page content to Apple's Private Cloud Compute, supporting 'Unneeded ... functionality of user applications are disabled'.
comments.open_question: Whether the feature is 'unneeded' is an organisational decision; confirm the organisation has not approved it.

comments.comment: The rule sets allowSafariSummary=false, disabling a user application feature, consistent with ISM-1470 and ruling 5.

items.final_note: Disables the Safari summary feature that sends page content off-device, where the organisation has decided it is unneeded.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Enterprise mobility > Organisation-owned mobile devices and desktop computers
items.ism_text: Personnel using organisation-owned mobile devices or desktop computers to access classified systems or data have enforced separation of classified data and personal data.
items.proposed_note: Stops organisational data on an organisation-owned Mac from syncing into a user's personal iCloud account; it does not by itself enforce separation of classified and personal data on the device.

comments.rationale: The control requires 'enforced separation of classified data and personal data' for personnel using organisation-owned desktop computers to access classified systems or data. Forcing iCloud sync off prevents classified data handled on the Mac from being mixed into the user's personal iCloud data store, which is part of that separation.
comments.open_question: Whether blocking sync to a personal cloud account is accepted as 'enforced separation', or whether ASD expects a device-level separation mechanism (separate profiles, managed containers) that these settings do not provide.

comments.comment: The rules block iCloud sync services, and one blocks Apple Account sign-in, preventing classified data flowing into a personal cloud store, which is one enforced element of separation. Partial coverage, stated in the note.

Research proposed mapping with note: Stops organisational data syncing to a personal iCloud account; it does not by itself separate classified and personal data on the device. Held for the maintainer: Does blocking personal iCloud sync count as separating classified and personal data (ISM-1482), or does ASD mean separate managed containers on the device?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Operating system exploit protection functionality is enabled.
items.proposed_note: Covers macOS's always-on memory exploit protections (ASLR, NX stack and heap), which cannot be turned off by configuration.

comments.rationale: The rule records that macOS inherently enforces ASLR, PIE, stack canaries and non-executable stack and heap, i.e. 'operating system exploit protection functionality is enabled'.
comments.open_question: The rule has no automated check or setting; it is an inherent-capability statement, so decide whether such rules should carry mappings.

comments.comment: The rule has no check and no fix (the fix text says the technology inherently meets this requirement), so it is attestation-only and excluded by ruling 4.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Operating system exploit protection functionality is enabled.
items.proposed_note: Keeps two macOS code-integrity protections (library validation and Apple Mobile File Integrity) switched on; other exploit protections are not covered.

comments.rationale: DisableLibraryValidation=false blocks loading of libraries not signed by Apple or the same team, and the AMFI rule ensures the amfi_get_out_of_my_way boot-arg is not set; both are OS protections against code injection, supporting 'Operating system exploit protection functionality is enabled'.
comments.open_question: ISM's 'exploit protection' wording derives from Windows Exploit Protection (DEP, ASLR, CFG and similar); it needs agreement that macOS code-signing enforcement counts as the equivalent.

comments.comment: Library validation (DisableLibraryValidation=false) and the AMFI boot-arg rule each have a check or fix and are OS-level exploit and code-injection protections. ISM-1492 does not define exploit protection in detail, so this is partial coverage.

Research proposed mapping with note: Keeps macOS library validation and Apple Mobile File Integrity enabled, which block loading of unsigned or foreign code; other exploit protections are not covered. Held for the maintainer: ISM 'exploit protection' usually means DEP/ASLR/CFG-style mitigations; do library validation and AMFI (code signing integrity) count?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Privileged access to systems
items.ism_text: Privileged access events are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: May record privileged (administrative) actions on the Mac locally; central forwarding is not covered.

comments.rationale: The rule adds the 'ad' (administrative) class to the audit_control flags; the mSCP discussion says this audits the execution of privileged functions, which relates to 'Privileged access events are centrally logged'. Whether 'ad' captures privileged access itself (such as sudo or admin authentication) rather than only certain administrative system calls is not established from the rule.
comments.open_question: Which events /etc/security/audit_event assigns to the 'ad' class on current macOS, and whether sudo and admin elevation events fall under 'ad' or under 'aa'.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Privileged access to systems
items.ism_text: Privileged access events are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Ensures sudo privilege escalation events are recorded on the device; forwarding them to a central log facility is not covered.

comments.rationale: The rule sets 'Defaults log_allowed' in sudoers and checks sudo -V, so every allowed privilege escalation via sudo is logged. This generates the 'privileged access events' the control requires.
comments.open_question: Decide whether producing the events locally counts as support when the control's key requirement is that they are 'centrally logged'.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > Data backup and restoration > Performing and retaining backups
items.ism_text: Backups of data, applications and settings are performed and retained in accordance with business criticality and business continuity requirements.
items.proposed_note: Turns on automatic Time Machine backups of the Mac; retention to business-criticality requirements is not addressed.

comments.rationale: Automatic Time Machine backups mean 'Backups of data, applications and settings are performed' for that Mac, but the control also requires performing and retaining them 'in accordance with business criticality and business continuity requirements', which is an organisational decision.
comments.open_question: Whether an organisation relying on Time Machine (rather than central backup) treats it as its backup mechanism for workstations; most will not.

comments.comment: The rule enforces automatic backups, meeting the 'backups are performed' part of the control; retention is an organisational matter, stated in the note.

items.final_note: Turns on automatic Time Machine backups; retention to business criticality and continuity requirements is not addressed.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Unprivileged access to systems
items.ism_text: Use of unprivileged access is centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Records logons and logoffs on the Mac, which is part of showing use of standard accounts; central forwarding and other activity are not covered.

comments.rationale: The 'lo' class records login and logout for all accounts, including unprivileged ones, which gives a partial record of 'Use of unprivileged access'. Whether logon/logoff events are enough to count as logging use of access is debatable.
comments.open_question: Whether assessors accept logon/logoff records as evidence of 'use of unprivileged access', or expect activity-level logging.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: Covers preventing users on Intel Macs from booting into recovery, single-user mode or other boot media to get around OS security settings.

comments.rationale: firmwarepasswd -check must report a firmware password is enabled, which blocks Option-key boot tools that could be used for 'bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems'.
comments.open_question: Intel-only (not supported on Apple Silicon), and the threat is physical-access bypass rather than the in-OS user rights the control mainly targets.

comments.comment: firmwarepasswd -check must report the password enabled, blocking boot-time bypass of OS security settings. Intel-only scope is stated.

items.final_note: Requires a firmware password so users on Intel Macs cannot boot recovery or other media to bypass OS security; not available on Apple Silicon.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: Covers stopping users from installing configuration profiles through the UI, so profiles come only from the organisation's MDM.

comments.rationale: allowUIConfigurationProfileInstallation=false blocks manual profile installation, preventing users adding profiles that could alter settings such as certificates, VPN or restrictions ('modifying security functionality of operating systems').
comments.open_question: MDM-delivered restrictions generally cannot be overridden by a user-installed profile anyway; confirm which security settings a manually installed profile could weaken.

comments.comment: allowUIConfigurationProfileInstallation=false prevents users adding profiles that could modify or weaken security configuration.

items.final_note: Stops users installing configuration profiles through the UI, so security settings change only through the organisation's MDM.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: macOS inherently blocks standard users from privileged functions such as disabling security safeguards; the rule records this rather than setting or checking anything.

comments.rationale: The rule states standard users cannot execute privileged functions, which it defines as including 'disabling, circumventing, or altering implemented security safeguards', closely matching 'Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems'.
comments.open_question: Whether a manual, attestation-only rule with no check or remediation counts as 'supporting' a control under this project's definition.

comments.comment: The rule has no check and its fix says the technology inherently meets the requirement, so it is attestation-only and excluded by ruling 4.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: Prevents users removing Apple Rapid Security Responses only.

comments.rationale: The restriction allowRapidSecurityResponseRemoval=false stops users removing installed Rapid Security Responses (vendor security mitigations), supporting 'Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality'.
comments.open_question: Decide whether an installed security patch counts as 'security functionality of operating systems'.

comments.comment: The rule only applies to macOS 15.0 and blocks removal of a security patch, which is patch management rather than preventing users bypassing, disabling or modifying OS security functionality. Apple replaced Rapid Security Response with Background Security Improvements, so the mechanism is also obsolete for current releases.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: Protects core macOS files and the system volume from modification; other security functionality is covered elsewhere.

comments.rationale: SIP (checked with csrutil status) and the read-only sealed system volume prevent any user, including root, from modifying protected OS components and audit tools, which supports 'Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems'.
comments.open_question: Unprivileged users are already blocked by file permissions; decide whether a protection aimed mainly at root and admin users counts toward a control worded about unprivileged users.

comments.comment: csrutil status and the sealed read-only system volume prevent modification of OS files and security tools, which covers unprivileged users as well.

items.final_note: Keeps System Integrity Protection on and the system volume read-only, so no user, including administrators, can modify protected OS security components.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality of operating systems.
items.proposed_note: Stops users rolling back Apple's Background Security Improvements (rapid security fixes).

comments.rationale: Rolling back a Background Security Improvement removes an applied security mitigation; blocking the rollback via DDM supports 'Unprivileged users are prevented from bypassing, disabling or modifying security functionality'.
comments.open_question: Whether removing an installed security patch is 'security functionality of operating systems' in the ISM sense, and whether the DDM restriction applies to standard users or to all users.

comments.comment: Blocking rollback of a Background Security Improvement stops removal of an installed patch, which is patch management rather than preventing users bypassing, disabling or modifying OS security functionality; it does not fit the control's intent.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > User application hardening > Web browsers
items.ism_text: Web browser security settings cannot be changed by human users.
items.proposed_note: Locks these two Safari security settings only.

comments.rationale: The rules deliver WarnAboutFraudulentWebsites=true and AutoOpenSafeDownloads=false in a com.apple.Safari configuration profile, so these Safari security settings are enforced by management rather than left to users, supporting 'Web browser security settings cannot be changed by human users'.
comments.open_question: Confirm that profile-managed com.apple.Safari keys are locked in Safari's Settings UI on the target macOS versions, rather than only set as defaults.

comments.comment: Both rules deliver and check keys in a com.apple.Safari configuration profile, and profile-managed Safari settings are enforced by management (greyed out for the user). Fit is partial since only two settings are locked.

items.final_note: Locks two Safari security settings only: the fraudulent website warning is on and automatic opening of 'safe' downloads is off.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Application management
items.ism_text: Unprivileged human users do not have the ability to install unapproved applications.
items.proposed_note: Blocks apps installed into user home folders only, using a control Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: Blocking execution from /Users/ stops standard users installing and running apps from their home folder, supporting 'Unprivileged human users do not have the ability to install unapproved applications'.
comments.open_question: Confirm the deprecated restriction still works, and whether other install paths available to standard users (such as the App Store) are blocked elsewhere.

comments.comment: The rule relies on com.apple.applicationaccess.new path deny lists (and the check reads the doubly deprecated pathBlackList key). Apple's device-management schema (https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.new.yaml) marks pathBlackList deprecated since 10.15, the path-list evaluation steps deprecated, and the whole payload deprecated in macOS 27.0; the rule's own discussion says it 'may not work as expected'. The check only tests that the preference exists, not that installs are blocked, and it blocks execution from /Users/ rather than installation. Rejected as an unreliable mechanism.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Credential management > Setting credentials for user accounts
items.ism_text: Credentials provided to human users are changed on first use.
items.proposed_note: Would cover changing an issued password on first use, but only if an administrator sets the flag on each account that is given a password.

comments.rationale: pwpolicy -setpolicy newPasswordRequired=1 forces the user to change the password at next logon, which is the mechanism for 'credentials provided to human users are changed on first use'. The mSCP rule has no check and no remediation ('technology inherently meets'), so it neither enforces nor verifies anything on its own.
comments.open_question: Decide whether an available-but-unenforced capability with no check is enough to count as supporting the control.

comments.comment: Attestation-only rule (manual, 'inherent', no check, no fix step). Ruling 4: not mapped.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Credential management > Protecting credentials
items.ism_text: Credentials are obscured as they are entered into systems.
items.proposed_note: macOS password fields always mask input; the rule records this inherent behaviour rather than setting or checking anything.

comments.rationale: The rule states macOS uses NSSecureTextField for password entry, which obscures typed characters, matching 'Credentials are obscured as they are entered into systems' almost word for word.
comments.open_question: Whether a manual, attestation-only rule with no check or remediation counts as 'supporting' a control under this project's definition.

comments.comment: Attestation-only rule (manual, 'inherent', check null, no fix). Ruling 4: not mapped.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for networking > Network design and configuration > Blocking anonymity network traffic
items.ism_text: Outbound network connections to anonymity networks are blocked.
items.proposed_note: Disables use of Apple's iCloud Private Relay from the device; it does not block outbound connections to other anonymity networks such as Tor.

comments.rationale: Private Relay is a two-hop relay that masks the user's IP address and destinations from network operators, functionally similar to the anonymity networks the control targets. Forcing allowCloudPrivateRelay false stops the device making those outbound relay connections, matching 'outbound network connections to anonymity networks are blocked' for this one service.
comments.open_question: Whether ASD regards iCloud Private Relay as an 'anonymity network' (the discussion names only Tor as an example), and whether a device-side restriction counts when the control is normally implemented at the network boundary.

comments.comment: ISM-1628 names Tor as the example; Private Relay is a two-hop relay that hides client IP and DNS, so it is functionally similar. The rule's check and profile (com.apple.applicationaccess allowCloudPrivateRelay=false, macOS 12+ per Apple's schema https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.yaml) directly block its use. Mapped on the same 'where the organisation has decided' basis as other disable rules.

Research proposed mapping with note: Disables use of iCloud Private Relay where the organisation treats it as an anonymity network; it does not block Tor or other anonymity networks. Held for the maintainer: Is iCloud Private Relay an 'anonymity network' for ISM-1628? The control discussion names only Tor.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Privileged access to systems
items.ism_text: Privileged user account and security group management events are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: May record user account and group changes on the Mac locally; central forwarding is not covered.

comments.rationale: The 'ad' class covers administrative actions such as changes to authentication policies; if it includes local account and group administration it supports 'Privileged user account and security group management events are centrally logged' at the source.
comments.open_question: Whether macOS account and group management (through opendirectoryd/dscl or System Settings) produces BSM events in the 'ad' class, or is only logged in the unified log.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Multi-factor authentication
items.ism_text: Multi-factor authentication used for authenticating human users of systems is phishing-resistant.
items.proposed_note: Would cover phishing resistance of multi-factor authentication to the Mac where a smartcard is enforced.

comments.rationale: Certificate-based smartcard authentication binds the private key to the card and is generally regarded as phishing-resistant. No ISM text in this repository names smart cards as phishing-resistant, and local console, su and sudo authentication is not a typical real-time phishing surface.
comments.open_question: Confirm against ASD's definition of phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (outside this repository) whether PIV/CAC-style smartcard authentication to a local workstation qualifies.

comments.comment: ASD guidance (https://www.cyber.gov.au/business-government/protecting-devices-systems/hardening-systems-applications/system-hardening/implementing-multi-factor-authentication) lists smart cards (PIV/PKI) as phishing-resistant, and Essential Eight allows them for workstation logon. enforceSmartCard drives enforcement; the PAM rules add smart card as an accepted method for each service.

items.final_note: Requires smart card authentication (card plus PIN), which ASD recognises as phishing-resistant MFA, for Mac login and screen unlock, and for su, sudo and login via PAM.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF applications, and security products are applied within one month of release.
items.proposed_note: Auto-updates App Store applications only; apps installed outside the App Store are not covered.

comments.rationale: Automatic App Store app updates support 'Patches ... in applications other than office productivity suites, web browsers ... are applied within one month of release' for App Store-delivered apps.
comments.open_question: Whether the organisation's apps are delivered through the App Store (many are not), and whether automatic updating without verification counts toward a time-bound control.

comments.comment: Check and fix are AutomaticallyInstallAppUpdates=true in com.apple.SoftwareUpdate. Automatic installation directly helps apply application patches within a month. That payload is removed in macOS 27 per Apple's schema, so this applies to macOS 15 and 26.

items.final_note: Automatically installs App Store application updates only; apps installed any other way are not covered, and the one-month timeframe is not verified.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release.
items.proposed_note: Limits how long macOS updates can be hidden by deferral; it does not force updates to be installed.

comments.rationale: The deferral cap of the ODV days (recommended 30) keeps updates from being withheld beyond a month, relating to 'applied within one month of release' for workstation operating systems.
comments.open_question: Same as for ism-1902: a deferral limit is not installation, and the payload is only defined for macOS 15.0.

comments.comment: enforcedSoftwareUpdateDelay is deprecated in macOS 26.0 and removed in 27.0 per Apple's schema (https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.yaml), and the rule's fix is only defined for macOS 15.0. A deferral cap also only limits how long updates are hidden and installs nothing. Rejected as a removed mechanism that does not apply updates.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release.
items.proposed_note: Automatically installs macOS updates, which supports the one-month window without guaranteeing it.

comments.rationale: Same mechanism as for ism-1902; ism-1695 is the Essential Eight ML1 form of the workstation OS patching requirement ('applied within one month of release').
comments.open_question: Same as for ism-1696: whether automatic installation without a verified timeframe counts toward a time-bound control.

comments.comment: Fix uses DDM com.apple.configuration.softwareupdate.settings AutomaticActions InstallOSUpdates and InstallSecurityUpdate AlwaysOn (plus legacy profile keys on macOS 15/26); checks read the matching settings. Automatic installation directly supports timely OS patching.

items.final_note: Automatically installs macOS updates and critical security updates, which supports the one-month window but does not verify it.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release.
items.proposed_note: Verifies that macOS last completed a full software update within ODV days (30 days in CIS/STIG, 7 in NLMAPGOV).

comments.rationale: Same mechanism as for ism-1902, against the Essential Eight ML1 wording 'applied within one month of release'.
comments.open_question: Whether LastFullSuccessfulDate reliably means all available updates were installed; the ODV must also be 30d or less.

comments.comment: Check reads LastFullSuccessfulDate in com.apple.SoftwareUpdate. Question: does it advance only when updates were actually installed, or on any successful update check? For installs: the fix runs softwareupdate -i -a and CIS audits treat it as 'software is current'. Against: no Apple source defines the key and it may update on a no-op scan; searches found no definition. A before/after test on a Mac would settle it. ODV must also be 30d or less for ISM-1695.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Covers automatic installation of Apple Background Security Improvements, which helps apply critical OS security fixes quickly.

comments.rationale: A DDM declaration enforces automatic installation of Background Security Improvements and prevents users changing it, helping 'patches ... for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations ... are applied within 48 hours of release'.
comments.open_question: Only covers Background Security Improvements, not full OS updates, and does not verify the 48-hour timeframe is met.

comments.comment: Fix is DDM RapidSecurityResponse Enable=true in com.apple.configuration.softwareupdate.settings and the check reads enableRapidSecurityResponse from the persisted DDM state (https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/declarative/declarations/configurations/softwareupdate.settings.yaml). Directly relevant to fast delivery of critical fixes.

items.final_note: Enforces automatic installation of Apple Background Security Improvements (macOS 27), which helps apply urgent OS security fixes quickly; it covers only these fixes and does not verify the 48-hour timeframe.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Allows Rapid Security Responses to install, enabling fast OS fixes; it does not enforce the 48-hour timeframe.

comments.rationale: allowRapidSecurityResponseInstallation=true ensures Apple's urgent OS mitigations are not blocked by policy, supporting applying 'vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations ... within 48 hours'.
comments.open_question: Allowing (rather than forcing) installation only removes a blocker and matches the default; a reviewer may consider this too indirect without a setting that enforces install deadlines.

comments.comment: Allowing Rapid Security Response (allowRapidSecurityResponseInstallation=true) only removes a blocker and is the default; no installation is enforced. Apple's schema (https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.yaml) shows the key deprecated in macOS 26.0 and removed in 27.0, and the rule applies to macOS 15 only. Rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical by vendors or when working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Automatically installs macOS security and OS updates, which makes the 48-hour window achievable but does not guarantee it.

comments.rationale: Enforcing automatic installation of security responses and macOS updates supports 'Patches ... in operating systems of workstations ... are applied within 48 hours of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as critical', but installation timing depends on the device being online, deferral settings and user restarts.
comments.open_question: Whether automatic installation without a verified deadline counts as support for a time-bound patching control; a DDM enforced-install deadline or a compliance check would be stronger evidence.

comments.comment: Same DDM AutomaticActions InstallOSUpdates and InstallSecurityUpdate AlwaysOn fix and checks as r056. InstallSecurityUpdate targets the urgent security updates this control is about, so it is partial but direct support.

items.final_note: Automatically installs macOS updates and critical security updates, making a 48-hour install achievable; the 48-hour deadline itself is not enforced.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Early Launch Antimalware, Secure Boot, Trusted Boot and Measured Boot functionality is enabled.
items.proposed_note: Covers booting macOS from a cryptographically signed and sealed system volume, which is comparable to the Secure Boot and Trusted Boot parts of the control.

comments.rationale: The check verifies csrutil authenticated-root is enabled, so the system volume is verified against Apple's signature at boot, providing the boot integrity that 'Secure Boot, Trusted Boot ... functionality is enabled' aims at.
comments.open_question: ISM-1745 names Windows features (Early Launch Antimalware, Measured Boot); decide whether macOS signed system volume verification is an accepted equivalent.

comments.comment: Check is the root mount being 'sealed' (or AuthenticatedRootVolumeEnabled on macOS 15) and the fix is csrutil authenticated-root enable. Signed system volume verification is part of Apple's boot chain of trust. Partial coverage, with the reader confirming equivalence.

items.final_note: Verifies macOS boots from a sealed, cryptographically signed system volume (Authenticated Root), the macOS counterpart of the Secure Boot and Trusted Boot parts of the control; it does not cover Windows-specific Early Launch Antimalware or Measured Boot.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for networking > Network design and configuration > Protective Domain Name System Services
items.ism_text: A protective DNS service is used to block access to known malicious domain names.
items.proposed_note: Keeps Safari's DNS lookups from being diverted to Apple's relay resolvers so the organisation's protective DNS service can see and block them; it does not configure or require a protective DNS service.
