comments.rationale: When Private Relay is on, Safari resolves names through Apple's relay (oblivious DNS-over-HTTPS) instead of the configured resolver, bypassing a protective DNS service. Forcing allowCloudPrivateRelay false removes that bypass, which helps 'a protective DNS service is used to block access to known malicious domain names' remain effective.
comments.open_question: This is indirect support (removing a bypass rather than providing the service); a reviewer needs to decide whether that is enough to count as 'supports'.

comments.comment: The rule enforces and checks allowCloudPrivateRelay=false (Apple schema, macOS 12+); its discussion notes Private Relay prevents enterprise traffic auditing. Removing this bypass is an enabling control for network-level DNS filtering. Partial and indirect, as the note states.

Research proposed mapping with note: Disables iCloud Private Relay so Safari DNS lookups are not diverted past the organisation's protective DNS service; it does not provide or require a protective DNS service. Held for the maintainer: Disabling iCloud Private Relay stops Safari DNS bypassing protective DNS but provides no protective DNS; is that support for ISM-1782?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > Data backup and restoration > Performing and retaining backups
items.ism_text: Backups of data, applications and settings are retained in a secure and resilient manner.
items.proposed_note: Encrypting the backup volume adds confidentiality; it does not make backups resilient (offline, immutable or off-site).

comments.rationale: Encrypted Time Machine volumes contribute to backups being 'retained in a secure ... manner', but nothing here addresses the 'resilient' part.
comments.open_question: Whether encryption of a local backup disk alone is enough to count as supporting 'secure and resilient' retention.

comments.comment: Check tests the TimeMachine plist for NotEncrypted and the fix is the documented Encrypt Backups steps. Encryption of backups is a direct security measure for retained backups.

items.final_note: Requires Time Machine backups to be encrypted, covering the 'secure' part of the control; it does not make backups offline, immutable or off-site.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for security assurance > Security monitoring > Centralised event logging facility
items.ism_text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion.
items.proposed_note: Covers preventing standard users from modifying local Apple System Log files.

comments.rationale: Root ownership and mode 640 mean only root can write the ASL log files, supporting 'event logs are protected from unauthorised modification and deletion' for those local files.
comments.open_question: Same section-scope question as ISM-1985 (centralised facility); deletion also depends on directory permissions, which these rules do not check.

comments.comment: Both rules check and fix file ownership and mode (macOS 15, 26, 27). ISM-1815 text covers protection of event logs from modification and deletion and does not itself require central logging, so local file protection is partial but direct support.

items.final_note: Sets ownership to root:wheel and mode 640 on the Apple System Log files listed in /etc/asl.conf and /etc/asl, so standard users cannot modify them; it does not check directory permissions or cover other logs.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Unprivileged access to systems
items.ism_text: Unprivileged access to systems and their resources is limited to only what is required for users to undertake their duties or functions.
items.proposed_note: Covers preventing users from browsing other users' home folders on the same Mac.

comments.rationale: The rules remove group and other access from each user's home folder (secure) or reset it to Apple's default restrictive permissions, limiting users' access to other users' data, part of 'unprivileged access to systems and their resources is limited'.
comments.open_question: ISM-1852 is about limiting access to what duties require, which is largely an account and role decision; decide whether file-system permissions on local home folders count as direct support.

comments.comment: os_home_folders_secure checks and fixes permissions with find and chmod; os_home_folders_default is a manual rule with a written check (ls -le /Users) and fix (diskutil resetUserPermissions). File-system access limiting is a technical measure restricting unprivileged access to resources.

items.final_note: Stops users reading other users' home folders on a shared Mac (home folders set to mode 700 or 711, or default permissions reset via diskutil); it does not decide who gets accounts.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Application control
items.ism_text: Application control is applied to user profiles and temporary folders used by operating systems, web browsers and email clients.
items.proposed_note: Blocks running apps from user home folders only, not temporary folders, using a control Apple has deprecated.

comments.rationale: The rule enables com.apple.applicationaccess.new familyControlsEnabled with pathBlackList /Users/, a path rule preventing software running from user profiles, which matches 'Application control is applied to user profiles ...'.
comments.open_question: The rule itself warns Apple deprecated these application restriction controls; confirm they still work, and note temporary folders are not covered.

comments.comment: Same mechanism as r048: path deny list in com.apple.applicationaccess.new, deprecated by Apple (pathBlackList deprecated 10.15, payload deprecated 27.0 per https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.new.yaml) and described by mSCP as possibly not working. It also does not cover temporary folders, only /Users/. Rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured to operate in a supervised (or equivalent) mode.
items.proposed_note: Verifies User Approved MDM enrolment, which gives Mac laptops supervised status on macOS 11 and later; desktops are not mobile devices.

comments.rationale: The check confirms 'MDM enrollment: Yes (User Approved)'; the rule discussion states that UAMDM grants Supervised status on macOS 11+, matching 'configured to operate in a supervised (or equivalent) mode'.
comments.open_question: Whether Mac laptops are in scope as mobile devices, and whether User Approved enrolment (as opposed to Automated Device Enrollment) is accepted as 'supervised (or equivalent)' on current macOS.

comments.comment: Apple states a Mac on macOS 11+ enrolled via device enrollment, or an upgraded Mac approved by a local admin, is supervised (https://support.apple.com/guide/deployment/about-device-supervision-dep1d89f0bff/web). Check greps for 'Yes (User Approved)'. Ruling 1 covers laptops.

items.final_note: Verifies the Mac is enrolled in MDM with User Approved enrolment, which makes a Mac on macOS 11 or later supervised; applies to Mac laptops only, as desktop Macs are not mobile devices.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured with secure password-based lock screens.
items.proposed_note: Requires a password to unlock the screen on Mac laptops; password strength is governed by other rules.

comments.rationale: Requiring authentication to dismiss the screen saver is a password-based lock screen, supporting 'Mobile devices are configured with secure password-based lock screens'.
comments.open_question: Two points: whether the organisation treats MacBooks as ISM 'mobile devices' (the ISM glossary is understood to include laptops, but no glossary is in the repo to verify this), and whether 'secure' also requires the password policy rules to be applied.

comments.comment: Check and fix are askForPassword=true in com.apple.screensaver (profile). Ruling 1: Mac laptops are mobile devices, so this is a password-based lock screen requirement.

items.final_note: On Mac laptops, requires a password to unlock the screen saver; password strength is governed by other rules.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Covers automatic installation of Apple Background Security Improvements, which helps apply OS security fixes within the required timeframe.

comments.rationale: A DDM declaration enforces automatic installation of Background Security Improvements, helping 'patches ... for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations ... are applied within one month of release'.
comments.open_question: Only covers Background Security Improvements, not full OS updates, and does not verify the timeframe is met.

comments.comment: Same DDM RapidSecurityResponse Enable=true check and fix as r058. Direct but partial support.

items.final_note: Enforces automatic installation of Apple Background Security Improvements (macOS 27), helping apply OS security fixes promptly; it covers only these fixes and does not verify the one-month timeframe.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Allows Rapid Security Responses to install; it does not enforce the one-month timeframe.

comments.rationale: allowRapidSecurityResponseInstallation=true ensures Apple's OS mitigations delivered as RSRs are not blocked, supporting applying OS patches 'within one month of release'.
comments.open_question: As for ISM-1696: enabling a delivery mechanism does not enforce a timeframe, and RSRs mostly target urgent rather than non-critical fixes.

comments.comment: Same as r059: allow-only setting that matches the default, enforces no installation, deprecated in macOS 26 and removed in 27 per Apple's schema (https://github.com/apple/device-management/blob/release/mdm/profiles/com.apple.applicationaccess.yaml), and the rule applies to macOS 15 only. Rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Limits how long macOS updates can be hidden by deferral; it does not force updates to be installed.

comments.rationale: The rule caps com.apple.applicationaccess enforcedSoftwareUpdateDelay at the ODV (recommended 30 days), so updates become available within about a month, which relates to OS patches being 'applied within one month of release'.
comments.open_question: Decide whether capping deferral counts as support when installation still depends on other update enforcement; also the payload is only defined for macOS 15.0.

comments.comment: Same as r055: enforcedSoftwareUpdateDelay is deprecated in macOS 26.0 and removed in 27.0 (Apple schema) and the fix is defined for macOS 15.0 only. A deferral cap does not install updates. Rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Automatically installs macOS updates, which supports the one-month window without guaranteeing it.

comments.rationale: Automatic installation of macOS and security updates supports 'Patches ... in operating systems of workstations ... are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical', subject to the device being online and restarting.
comments.open_question: Same as for ism-1696: whether automatic installation without a verified timeframe counts toward a time-bound control.

comments.comment: Same DDM AutomaticActions InstallOSUpdates and InstallSecurityUpdate AlwaysOn fix and checks as r056.

items.final_note: Automatically installs macOS updates and critical security updates, which supports the one-month window but does not verify it.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Automatic checking and downloading are prerequisites for timely patching; they do not install anything.

comments.rationale: Enforcing automatic update checks and downloads shortens the path to 'applied within one month of release', but applying the patch still depends on the install rules or the user.
comments.open_question: Whether prerequisite settings that do not apply patches should be mapped at all; they may be better left unmapped.

comments.comment: Check and fix are AutomaticCheckEnabled and AutomaticDownload (DDM AutomaticActions Download AlwaysOn also available). Prerequisites for timely patching, so partial support. The AutomaticCheckEnabled profile key is removed in macOS 27 per Apple's schema.

Research proposed mapping with note: Turns on automatic update checking and downloading so updates are ready to install; it does not itself install anything. Held for the maintainer: Automatic update checking and downloading installs nothing; does it support the one-month patch control, or only the install-enforcing rules?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system management > System maintenance > Mitigating known vulnerabilities
items.ism_text: Patches, updates or other vendor mitigations for vulnerabilities in operating systems of workstations, non-internet-facing servers and non-internet-facing network devices are applied within one month of release when vulnerabilities are assessed as non-critical by vendors and no working exploits exist.
items.proposed_note: Verifies that macOS last completed a full software update within ODV days (30 days in CIS/STIG, 7 in NLMAPGOV).

comments.rationale: If the last full successful Software Update was within 30 days, OS updates released more than a month ago should already be installed, which verifies 'applied within one month of release'.
comments.open_question: Whether LastFullSuccessfulDate reliably means all available updates were installed (rather than only a successful scan); the ODV must also be 30d or less.

comments.comment: Same question as r057: does LastFullSuccessfulDate (com.apple.SoftwareUpdate) record a successful scan or a completed install? For installs: the fix is softwareupdate -i -a and CIS treats it as 'current'. Against: no Apple documentation defines it and searches found none. A before/after test on a Mac would settle it. ODV must be 30d or less for ISM-1902.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Operating system event logging
items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Records some administrative actions on the Mac locally; central forwarding is not covered.

comments.rationale: The 'ad' flag in audit_control records administrative action events, and the control's discussion lists 'changes to security policies' as a typical security-relevant macOS event; the mSCP rule cites modifying authentication policies as an 'ad' event. The exact event set in the class is not verified here.
comments.open_question: Confirm from /etc/security/audit_event that the 'ad' class includes security policy changes on current macOS versions.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Operating system event logging
items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Records file access and program execution events on the Mac locally (mostly failed attempts); central forwarding is not covered.

comments.rationale: The checks verify '-fr', '-fw', '-fm', '-fd' and '-ex' (failed file read, write, attribute change, attribute delete and program execution) and 'fm' (all attribute changes) in the audit_control flags. Denied access attempts are arguably security-relevant events, but the control's discussion list does not name file access, and failed execution is not the same as the 'successful process creations' it does list.
comments.open_question: Whether file access failure events count as 'security-relevant events' for ISM-1976 in the organisation's logging policy; the discussion list is 'typical' rather than exhaustive.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Operating system event logging
items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Covers generating detailed Application Firewall log events on the Mac; sending them to a central log store is not covered.

comments.rationale: EnableLogging=true with LoggingOption=detail makes the macOS Application Firewall write events to unified logging, a prerequisite for 'security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged'.
comments.open_question: The control requires central logging; local logging only helps indirectly. Firewall events are also marked private unless a separate profile is applied.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Operating system event logging
items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Ensures sudo privilege escalation events are recorded on the device; central collection is not covered.

comments.rationale: sudo log_allowed makes allowed privilege escalations appear in the macOS log, a security-relevant macOS event source for 'Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged'.
comments.open_question: Decide whether local event generation for one event type counts as support for a control whose substance is central logging.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for security assurance > Security monitoring > Centralised event logging facility
items.ism_text: Event logs are protected from unauthorised access.
items.proposed_note: Covers restricting read access to local Apple System Log files to root and the wheel group.

comments.rationale: The rules set ASL log files listed in /etc/asl.conf to root:wheel ownership and mode 640 or less, so standard users cannot read them, matching 'event logs are protected from unauthorised access' for those local files.
comments.open_question: ISM-1985 sits under 'Centralised event logging facility', so it may be intended for the central log store rather than local host logs; ASL is also largely superseded by unified logging on modern macOS.

comments.comment: Same checks and fixes as r064. ISM-1985 text is about protecting event logs from unauthorised access and does not require a central store; the rule does not forward logs, so only local file protection is claimed.

items.final_note: Restricts Apple System Log files listed in /etc/asl.conf and /etc/asl to root:wheel with mode 640, so standard users cannot read them; local logs only.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for security assurance > Security monitoring > Event log retention
items.ism_text: Event logs are retained in a searchable manner for at least 12 months.
items.proposed_note: Sets how long the Mac keeps its local audit trail; only helps if set to at least 12 months, and local files are not easily searchable.

comments.rationale: The rule sets 'expire-after' in /etc/security/audit_control to an organisation-defined value. The control requires 'Event logs are retained in a searchable manner for at least 12 months'. Shipped benchmark values are 7d, 60d and 180d, and a size limit (for example '60d OR 5G') can expire logs earlier, so the default configuration does not meet the control; retention is normally achieved in the central facility.
comments.open_question: Whether the organisation sets expire-after to 12 months or more without a size cap, and whether local BSM files (searchable with auditreduce/praudit) count as 'searchable'.

comments.comment: Check and fix edit expire-after in /etc/security/audit_control (benchmark ODVs such as 60d OR 5G, 7d or 180d would not meet 12 months). Local BSM audit files are searchable with auditreduce and praudit.

items.final_note: Keeps local audit records for the configured expire-after period; supports this control only if set to 365d or more, and without an 'OR' size cap that deletes sooner.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for security assurance > Security monitoring > Event log retention
items.ism_text: Event logs are retained in a searchable manner for at least 12 months.
items.proposed_note: Keeps the local install.log for the configured number of days; only meets the 12-month minimum when that value is 365 or more, and covers that one log only.

comments.rationale: The rule sets and checks the aslmanager TTL for /var/log/install.log to be at least $ODV days (recommended 365). With ODV >= 365 this directly makes one event log be 'retained ... for at least 12 months'.
comments.open_question: The ODV validation allows values as low as 1, so support depends on the deployed value; also whether a single local software-install log, rather than a centralised searchable store, is what a reviewer accepts as 'event logs are retained in a searchable manner'.

comments.comment: Check and fix set ttl on /var/log/install.log via aslmanager config; ODV recommended 365, validation min 1. The text-based install.log is searchable.

items.final_note: Keeps the local install.log for the configured number of days; meets 12 months only when set to 365 or more, and covers that one log only.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Screen locking
items.ism_text: Systems are configured with a screen lock that:
items.proposed_note: Sets display sleep to 10 minutes or less on Apple Silicon laptops; it does not itself require a password on wake.

comments.rationale: The rule sets pmset displaysleep to 10 minutes or less and sleep to 15 minutes or less, within the control's 'maximum of 15 minutes of human user inactivity', and keeps display sleep shorter than system sleep.
comments.open_question: Display sleep only locks the screen if a password is required on wake, which is set by a different rule; decide whether this timer alone counts as support.

comments.comment: Check reads pmset values (battery) on Apple Silicon MacBooks and the fix sets pmset -a sleep 15 and displaysleep 10. With a password required immediately on wake, display sleep conceals the screen within the 15 minute limit. Partial and dependent on the password rule.

items.final_note: Sets display sleep to 10 minutes or less and system sleep to 15 minutes or less on Apple Silicon MacBooks; counts as a screen lock only when a password is also required on wake.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Screen locking
items.ism_text: Systems are configured with a screen lock that:
items.proposed_note: Ensures only the session owner can unlock a locked screen; other screen lock requirements are covered elsewhere.

comments.rationale: The rule sets the system.login.screensaver authorization rule to authenticate-session-owner (screenUnlockMode), so administrators cannot unlock another user's locked session, supporting the 'requires re-authentication by human users ... to unlock the system' part.
comments.open_question: Decide whether restricting who can unlock is part of the control, which is about the re-authentication requirement itself.

comments.comment: Fix is com.apple.loginwindow screenUnlockMode=1 and the check reads the authorization db rule authenticate-session-owner. It strengthens the re-authentication requirement, partial support.

items.final_note: Ensures only the session owner can unlock a locked screen, so re-authentication is by the user who locked it; other screen lock requirements are covered elsewhere.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Screen locking
items.ism_text: Systems are configured with a screen lock that:
items.proposed_note: Removes Apple Watch and Touch ID as alternative ways to unlock, so unlocking falls back to the account's primary credential.

comments.rationale: The control requires unlocking with 're-authentication by human users using all authentication factors'. An Apple Watch proximity unlock or a fingerprint alone lets the user skip the full credential; disabling them pushes unlock back to the password or smart card.
comments.open_question: Whether removing alternative single-factor unlock methods counts as enforcing 'all authentication factors', given the remaining macOS unlock is typically still a single password unless smart card enforcement is also configured.

comments.comment: Check and fix are allowAutoUnlock=false and allowFingerprintForUnlock=false in com.apple.applicationaccess. Supports the re-authentication with all authentication factors requirement by removing alternative unlock methods.

items.final_note: Removes Apple Watch and Touch ID as ways to unlock the screen, so unlocking requires the account's primary credential rather than a single-factor shortcut.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Screen locking
items.ism_text: Systems are configured with a screen lock that:
items.proposed_note: Removes a hot corner that would prevent the screen lock from starting; it does not stop users re-adding it.

comments.rationale: A hot corner set to 'Disable Screen Saver' lets a user suppress the inactivity lock; removing it supports 'denies human users the ability to disable the screen locking mechanism'. However the check and fix act on the current user's own com.apple.dock preferences rather than a managed profile, so the user can reconfigure it afterwards.
comments.open_question: Whether the deployment enforces this through a managed profile (which would actually deny the user the ability) or only remediates the user preference after the fact.

comments.comment: Check inspects wvous-*-corner prefs of the last user and the fix deletes them (no profile enforcement). Partial support for keeping the screen lock active.

Research proposed mapping with note: Removes hot corners that could disable the screen saver for the last logged-in user; it is a one-off cleanup that users can undo. Held for the maintainer: This rule only clears existing hot corners once and users can re-add them; does it support the 'cannot be disabled' screen lock requirement?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Credential management > Password strength
items.ism_text: Passwords appearing in lists of commonly used passwords or lists of compromised passwords are not used.
items.proposed_note: Would partly cover the control by rejecting passwords made of repeated or sequential characters, a common subset of compromised passwords, without checking against an actual password list.

comments.rationale: allowSimple=false / RequireComplexPasscode=true rejects repeating, ascending and descending character sequences (for example 1111 or abcd); it is not a character-class rule, so it does not conflict with ISM-2080. The mSCP note says it 'prevents use of passwords which are regularly found in compromised password lists'. The control requires that passwords 'appearing in lists of commonly used passwords or lists of compromised passwords are not used', which is a list check this setting does not perform.
comments.open_question: Decide whether a pattern-based block of trivially guessable passwords counts as partial support for a list-based control.

comments.comment: allowSimple=false blocks repeating and sequential characters, a complexity rule, not a check against lists of common or compromised passwords. ISM-2078 is specifically list-based, so this does not meet the control's intent. Rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured to enforce separation between organisational and personal mobile applications and data.
items.proposed_note: Stops organisational files, mail, contacts, calendars, notes, photos, bookmarks and passwords on the Mac from syncing into a user's personal iCloud account; it does not separate personal and organisational apps or data on the device itself.

comments.rationale: Disabling iCloud sync (and Apple Account sign-in) removes the main built-in path by which organisational data on a Mac would be copied into a personal Apple account, which is one aspect of 'enforce separation between organisational and personal mobile applications and data'.
comments.open_question: Two points: (1) whether ISM's 'mobile devices' covers macOS laptops (the ISM glossary is not in this repo to confirm; ASD's published glossary is understood to include notebook computers, unverified here); (2) whether ASD intends 'separation' to mean managed/unmanaged app and data containers, which blocking iCloud sync does not provide, rather than blocking flows to personal cloud storage.

comments.comment: Each rule enforces an allowCloud* restriction in com.apple.applicationaccess (or hides the Apple Account pane) and checks it. Ruling 1 treats Mac laptops as mobile devices. Partial support for data separation.

Research proposed mapping with note: On Mac laptops, stops organisational files, mail, contacts, calendars, notes, photos, bookmarks, passwords and desktop/documents from syncing into a personal iCloud account; it does not separate personal and organisational apps on the device. Held for the maintainer: Does blocking personal iCloud sync count as enforced separation of organisational and personal apps and data on laptops (ISM-2096)?

items.ism_section: Guidelines for media > Media usage > Encrypting media
items.ism_text: Pre-boot authentication using passwords, or managed network-based key release, is implemented for media containing encrypted system volumes.
items.proposed_note: Covers pre-boot password authentication for the internal startup volume only.

comments.rationale: With FileVault enabled, a user password must be entered at startup before the encrypted volume is unlocked, which matches 'Pre-boot authentication using passwords ... is implemented for media containing encrypted system volumes'.
comments.open_question: Decide whether enforcing FileVault is enough to count as pre-boot authentication, given that unattended restarts (fdesetup authrestart) bypass the prompt and the rule does not check for them.

comments.comment: Check and fix are ForceEnableInSetupAssistant in com.apple.MCX.FileVault2. FileVault requires a user password before the volume unlocks at boot; ruling 2 accepts FileVault as approved cryptography.

items.final_note: Enforces FileVault enablement at Setup Assistant, giving pre-boot password authentication for the internal startup volume; it does not test for unattended restarts that bypass the prompt.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Digital signature verification functionality for drivers is enforced before they are loaded.
items.proposed_note: Ensures macOS code-signature enforcement is not switched off, which underpins signature checks on kernel extensions; it does not configure driver policy itself.

comments.rationale: AMFI is the kernel component that enforces code signatures; checking that amfi_get_out_of_my_way=1 is absent keeps signature verification active, supporting 'Digital signature verification functionality for drivers is enforced before they are loaded'.
comments.open_question: Whether AMFI is the mechanism that verifies kext/driver signatures on current macOS, or whether kext signing is enforced independently (e.g. by SIP and kernel policy), in which case this rule does not support the control.

comments.comment: Check is only that boot-args does not include amfi_get_out_of_my_way=1. No Apple primary source ties AMFI to driver or kext signature verification; Apple documents kext signing as enforced via SIP and security policy (https://support.apple.com/guide/security/securely-extending-the-kernel-sec8e454101b/1/web/1). Too indirect, rejected.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Hardening operating system configurations
items.ism_text: Digital signature verification functionality for drivers is enforced before they are loaded.
items.proposed_note: Covers kernel extension signing enforcement only.

comments.rationale: With SIP enabled, macOS enforces kernel extension signing; disabling SIP is what allows unsigned kexts to load. This relates to 'Digital signature verification functionality for drivers is enforced before they are loaded'.
comments.open_question: Confirm against Apple platform security documentation that SIP status is what governs kext signature enforcement on current macOS versions.

comments.comment: Apple's Platform Security guide states that turning off SIP inactivates kext signature enforcement (https://support.apple.com/guide/security/securely-extending-the-kernel-sec8e454101b/1/web/1). Check is csrutil status.

items.final_note: Keeps System Integrity Protection enabled, which enforces kernel extension signature verification.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Credential management > Revoking credentials
items.ism_text: Credentials for user accounts are revoked when they are no longer required.
items.proposed_note: Would cover the device side of credential revocation: a revoked smartcard certificate can no longer be used to log on to the Mac.

comments.rationale: checkCertificateTrust=3 requires a positive CRL/OCSP response (hard fail) before smartcard authentication succeeds, so a credential revoked at the CA is refused at the Mac. The control text 'credentials for user accounts are revoked when they are no longer required' is about the act of revoking, which happens at the CA, not on the device.
comments.open_question: Decide whether enforcing revocation status at authentication counts as supporting a control about revoking credentials, or whether the control is purely an identity-management process.

comments.comment: Check and fix are checkCertificateTrust=3 in com.apple.security.smartcard. This is device-side enforcement of credential revocation; the identity process that revokes credentials is outside this rule.

items.final_note: Requires a verified positive OCSP/CRL response (hard revocation) for smart card authentication, so a revoked certificate cannot be used to log on to the Mac.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Credential management > Revoking credentials
items.ism_text: Credentials for user accounts are revoked when they are no longer required.
items.proposed_note: Would cover the device side of credential revocation, but only when the CRL/OCSP responder is reachable.

comments.rationale: checkCertificateTrust=2 performs soft-fail revocation checking: a certificate known to be revoked is refused, but authentication still succeeds if the CRL/OCSP server is unreachable. The control is about revoking credentials when no longer required, which happens at the CA rather than on the device.
comments.open_question: Same question as the high-trust rule, plus whether soft-fail checking is strong enough to count at all.

comments.comment: Check and fix are checkCertificateTrust=2 in com.apple.security.smartcard. Partial support: revocation is honoured when the responder is reachable.

items.final_note: Checks smart card certificate revocation (CRL/OCSP) at logon so a revoked certificate is refused, but authentication still succeeds if the responder is unreachable (soft fail).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system access > Identity and access management > Single-factor authentication
items.ism_text: Successful and unsuccessful single-factor authentication events are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Records successful and unsuccessful sign-in events on the Mac itself; forwarding them to a central logging facility is not covered.

comments.rationale: Committed as confident in 8b6d687 for local event generation.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix). Removed from baselines/_mappings/rules/.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for system hardening > Operating system hardening > Operating system event logging
items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Turns on and verifies the macOS security audit service that generates the security-relevant event records; sending them to a central logging facility is not covered.

comments.rationale: Committed as confident in 8b6d687 for local event generation.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix). Removed from baselines/_mappings/rules/.

items.ism_text: Security-relevant events for Apple macOS operating systems are centrally logged.
items.proposed_note: Records macOS authentication, authorisation and logon/logoff events locally; forwarding them to a central logging facility is not covered.

comments.rationale: Committed as confident in 8b6d687 for local event generation.

comments.comment: Rejected on the maintainer's ruling (2026-10-30): local logging is not central logging. A rule that produces or keeps logs on the Mac only supports a 'centrally logged' control when paired with something that forwards those logs to a central service, and mSCP has no such rule (audit_off_load_records states the technology does not support it and has no check or fix). items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted storage
items.ism_text: Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage and any removable media using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops are required to have FileVault on and all internal storage volumes encrypted.

comments.comment: FileVault (AES-XTS-256, NIAP certified against the Full Drive Encryption cPPs) is ASD-approved cryptography per the maintainer ruling. These rules satisfy 'encrypt their internal storage'. Removable media is covered by a separate entry.

items.final_note: Mac laptops are required to have FileVault on and all internal storage volumes encrypted.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted storage
items.ism_text: Mobile devices encrypt their internal storage and any removable media using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops are required to have every external APFS or HFS+ storage volume encrypted.

comments.comment: Checks that external volumes use APFS/HFS+ encryption (AES-XTS-256, ASD-approved per the maintainer ruling). Satisfies 'any removable media' for APFS and HFS+ volumes only; other formats such as exFAT or FAT cannot be encrypted by this setting.

items.final_note: Mac laptops are required to have every external APFS or HFS+ storage volume encrypted.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured with secure password-based lock screens.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops lock automatically after inactivity and require a password to unlock.

comments.comment: The screen saver starts after the configured inactivity timeout and a password is required to unlock it after the configured delay, giving a password-based lock screen. Covers 'lock screens' and 'password-based'; password strength is covered by a separate entry.

items.final_note: Mac laptops lock automatically after inactivity and require a password to unlock.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured with secure password-based lock screens.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops must use a password of at least the configured minimum length, so the lock screen password is not trivially short.

comments.comment: The lock screen password is the account password, so the minimum length policy covers the 'secure' part of 'secure password-based lock screens'. The length must be the organisation's chosen minimum because the ISM does not fix a number here.

items.final_note: Mac laptops must use a password of at least the configured minimum length, so the lock screen password is not trivially short.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Security updates are applied to mobile devices as soon as they become available.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops install security and macOS updates automatically so they are patched soon after release.

comments.comment: Automatic install of critical security updates and macOS updates, plus a check that the Mac is current, directly implement 'security updates are applied as soon as they become available'. They cover Apple OS and bundled-component updates, not third-party applications.
Merge: dropped system_settings_software_update_enforce (automatic checking installs nothing; see r073).

items.final_note: Mac laptops install security and macOS updates automatically so they are patched soon after release.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Security updates are applied to mobile devices as soon as they become available.
items.proposed_note: On Mac laptops, software updates may be deferred only up to a set number of days.

comments.comment: The rule caps the deferral at an ODV number of days; any deferral above 0 delays updates beyond 'as soon as they become available'. Question: does a bounded deferral (for example 7 days) count as supporting 'as soon as', or must it be 0 days to be mapped? For: it limits delay and allows compatibility testing. Against: the control wording has no allowance for delay.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured to operate in a supervised (or equivalent) mode.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops must be enrolled in MDM with user-approved enrolment, which makes them supervised.

comments.comment: User-approved MDM enrolment or ADE enrolment gives a Mac supervised status on macOS 11 and later, per the rule discussion. The rule checks for 'Yes (User Approved)' enrolment, matching 'supervised (or equivalent) mode'.

items.final_note: Mac laptops must be enrolled in MDM with user-approved enrolment, which makes them supervised.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured with remote locate and wipe functionality.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops enrolled in MDM with Location Services on can be remotely located, locked and wiped.

comments.comment: MDM enrolment provides the channel for remote lock and wipe, and Location Services must be on for locating, but neither rule checks that a locate or wipe function is configured. Question: is a device-side prerequisite (MDM enrolment plus Location Services) enough to count as 'configured with remote locate and wipe', or does it need a rule that verifies the lock and wipe capability itself? system_settings_find_my_disable deliberately turns off Find My in favour of MDM, so it is not mapped.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices prevent personnel from installing non-approved applications once provisioned.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops do not let standard users install software.

comments.comment: Standard users are blocked from installing software, so only administrators or the MDM can add applications once the Mac is provisioned. Matches 'prevent personnel from installing non-approved applications'; installs by administrators or MDM are by definition approved.
Rejected at merge: the rule's fix uses the deprecated pathBlackList key, and the same rule was rejected for ISM-1592 and ISM-1870 (r048, r066) for that reason.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices prevent personnel from installing non-approved applications once provisioned.
items.proposed_note: On Mac laptops, Gatekeeper only allows apps from the App Store or identified developers, and users cannot override it.

comments.comment: Gatekeeper with override disallowed stops users running unsigned or unidentified-developer software. Question: 'non-approved' means approved by the organisation, but the Gatekeeper allow list is Apple's (App Store or any Developer ID), so should this count as supporting 0863 or only as a partial control? For: it blocks a large class of unapproved software without admin action. Against: any Developer ID app is still allowed.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices prevent personnel from disabling or modifying security functionality once provisioned.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops stop users from overriding Gatekeeper, installing their own configuration profiles, or turning off System Integrity Protection.

comments.comment: Each prevents a user weakening security functionality that MDM provisioned: Gatekeeper cannot be overridden, profiles can only come from the MDM, and SIP protects system files and security tooling from modification. Together they satisfy 'prevent personnel from disabling or modifying security functionality' in part; settings not covered by these rules remain user-changeable.

items.final_note: Mac laptops stop users from overriding Gatekeeper, installing their own configuration profiles, or turning off System Integrity Protection.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices prevent personnel from disabling or modifying security functionality once provisioned.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops are protected by a recovery lock (Apple silicon) or firmware password (Intel) so users cannot change startup security.

comments.comment: Recovery lock and firmware password restrict recovery mode, Startup Manager and the startup security utility, where SIP and Secure Boot policy could otherwise be altered. Covers 'disabling or modifying security functionality' at the boot level; the recovery lock applies to Apple silicon and the firmware password to Intel.

items.final_note: Mac laptops are protected by a recovery lock (Apple silicon) or firmware password (Intel) so users cannot change startup security.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted storage
items.ism_text: SECRET and TOP SECRET mobile devices do not use removable media unless approved beforehand by ASD.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops used with SECRET or TOP SECRET data block removable storage media.

comments.comment: The rule denies mounting of removable storage (USB drives, optical media), which satisfies 'do not use removable media'. The ASD pre-approval exception in the control would be handled by not applying the rule to approved devices.
Rejected at merge: the rule's fix uses the deprecated com.apple.systemuiserver mount-controls payload, and the same rule was rejected for ISM-1418 (r031) for that reason.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured to prevent data transfers over Universal Serial Bus connections.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops block mounting USB storage devices and disk images, limiting data transfer over USB.

comments.comment: Blocking removable storage closes USB mass storage transfers. Question: the control says 'prevent data transfers over Universal Serial Bus connections' in general, but these rules do not stop other USB data paths such as tethering, MTP or phone file transfer, so is partial USB mass-storage blocking enough to map? system_settings_usb_restricted_mode (authorise accessories, block while locked) adds some support but is not a transfer block.
Rejected at merge: both rules rely on the deprecated mount-controls payload, already rejected elsewhere (r031).

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device usage > Using Bluetooth functionality
items.ism_text: Bluetooth functionality is not enabled on SECRET and TOP SECRET mobile devices.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops keep Bluetooth off unless an approved device is connected (SECRET and TOP SECRET control).

comments.comment: The rule turns Bluetooth off when no approved device is connected. Question: the control says Bluetooth 'is not enabled' on SECRET and TOP SECRET devices, but this rule allows Bluetooth while an approved device is connected, so does it support the control or would only a rule disabling Bluetooth unconditionally qualify? For: Bluetooth is off in the common case. Against: Bluetooth can be on, which the control forbids outright.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device usage > Maintaining control of mobile devices
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are carried or stored in a secured state when not being actively used.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops lock automatically when idle and discard the FileVault key on hibernate, so an idle laptop is in a secured state.

comments.comment: Automatic lock and destroying the FileVault key on standby leave an unattended Mac locked or encrypted at rest. Question: 'carried or stored in a secured state' is mainly a physical handling control, so does an enforced lock and key discard count as the secured state the control requires? For: it sets a locked or encrypted state without user action. Against: the ISM may expect the device to be powered off or physically secured.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Encrypted communications
items.ism_text: Mobile devices encrypt all sensitive or classified data communicated over public network infrastructure using ASD-approved cryptography.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops only use FIPS-validated encryption algorithms for SSH connections, covering SSH traffic over public networks.

comments.comment: Restricts the SSH client and server to FIPS 140 validated ciphers, key exchange and MACs, matching 'ASD-approved cryptography' as already accepted for other ISM cryptography controls. Covers SSH only; other protocols carrying sensitive data over public networks are not enforced by these rules.

items.final_note: Mac laptops only use FIPS-validated encryption algorithms for SSH connections, covering SSH traffic over public networks.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device management > Maintaining mobile device security
items.ism_text: Mobile devices are configured to enforce separation between organisational and personal mobile applications and data.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops block personal Apple Account sign-in and iCloud document sync, keeping organisational data away from personal accounts.

comments.comment: Blocking the Apple Account, internet account changes and iCloud Drive sync prevents organisational files syncing into personal cloud storage. Question: the control asks for enforced separation between organisational and personal apps and data, so does blocking personal accounts count as separation or only as an alternative to it? For: removes the main personal data path. Against: it does not separate personal apps and local data on the same Mac.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Enterprise mobility > Organisation-owned mobile devices and desktop computers
items.ism_text: Personnel using organisation-owned mobile devices or desktop computers to access classified systems or data have enforced separation of classified data and personal data.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops block personal Apple Account sign-in and iCloud document sync, keeping classified data away from personal accounts.

comments.comment: Same mechanism as for ISM-2096: personal accounts and iCloud sync cannot be used, so classified files do not flow into personal storage. Question: does blocking personal accounts count as 'enforced separation of classified data and personal data' on organisation-owned Macs, or is a managed data boundary required? For: closes the main personal sync path. Against: personal files can still sit alongside classified data on the Mac.

items.ism_section: Guidelines for enterprise mobility > Mobile device usage > Using paging, message services and messaging apps
items.ism_text: Paging, Multimedia Message Service, Short Message Service and messaging apps are not used to communicate sensitive or classified data.
items.proposed_note: Mac laptops block the built-in Messages app, so SMS, MMS and iMessage cannot be used on them for sensitive data.

comments.comment: The rule blocks launching Messages.app, which carries iMessage and SMS relay on the Mac. This covers Short Message Service and Apple messaging; third-party messaging apps are not blocked by this rule.

items.final_note: Mac laptops block the built-in Messages app, so SMS, MMS and iMessage cannot be used on them for sensitive data.
